properties.snippet: Potential Hurricane Refuge Area
properties.description:
City and County of Honolulu

Department of Emergency Management

Oahu Hurricane Refuge Areas

Not every Hurricane Refuge Area will open during an emergency. Depending on the circumstances, the City may use facilities other than those listed here. Specific locations and opening times will be determined based on the situation and will broadcast over local radio, TV, and official social media sites. 


Hurricane Refuge Areas are intended to be a last resort for those without safer options. In almost all cases, these facilities—often referred to as “shelters”—do NOT meet State of Hawaii guidelines for hurricane evacuation shelters. Structural engineers have evaluated “best available refuge areas,” which may be safer than remaining in areas prone to flooding, storm surge, or in older homes with wood frames or single-wall construction.


Whenever possible, the public should plan to shelter-in-place with family or friends in homes outside of these hazard areas that were designed, built, or renovated to better withstand hurricane conditions. Based on building codes, Oahu homes with plans dated 1994 or later and built 1995 or later should have additional protective measures in place. Homeowners are also encouraged to retrofit their homes to make them safer for sheltering.


Hurricane Refuge Areas are not stocked with supplies. If you choose to relocate to a Hurricane Refuge Area, plan to take as much of your emergency supply kit as possible with you. Include food, water, clothing, medications, and personal hygiene supplies, as well as a mat or cot. You may have 10 square feet per person or less, depending on the number of evacuees. If you bring pets with you, you will need to provide crates or carriers of appropriate sizes and other essential items such as cleaning supplies.


Additional Resources: Homeowner’s Handbook to Prepare for Natural Hazards produced by the University of Hawaii Sea Grant College Program (Hawaii Sea Grant).

properties.snippet: National Wildlife Refuge centroids joined to counts of federally-listed threatened or endangered species that may be found there
properties.description:
Defenders of Wildlife and the National Wildlife Refuge Association pored over hundreds of federal documents—with a focus on refuge Comprehensive Conservation Plans (CCP)—to develop an up-to-date list of species found on or dependent on units of the National Wildlife Refuge System. Refuge unit boundaries from the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service's cadastral dataset were used. The full dataset backing this report, as well as a copy of every CCP available, is available here.

Sources. To compile the list of ESA-listed species on the NWRS, we collected and reviewed official government documents from a variety of online and offline resources. Typically, the Comprehensive Conservation Plans (CCPs) required of all NWRS units were the primary source of information. Many of these are not yet available online, so we acquired copies from FWS staff by calling or emailing the request. We also mined other official documents. For example, we used the FWS's ECOS website, which houses key administrative documents on all ESA-listed species, as a primary source. We also used ESAdocs Search to search additional official documents, many of which are not yet available from government websites. We ran all documents that lacked a text layer in the PDF through optical character recognition software to enable searching. Last, we used the FWS's in-house dataset of ESA-listed species on NWRS units as an initial list to build on or filter as needed.

Data collection. After getting a complete tally of the units of the NWRS (see Compiled data, below), one member of the team began a "quick-and-dirty" initial pass of the refuges and the document sets. This allowed an evaluation of the variation among document types, writing styles, etc.

Next, we randomly assigned each unit to members of the project team. Each person reviewed the initial list of species on refuges from the FWS dataset, then began reviewing CCPs and other documents. A species (following the ESA's definition of species, i.e., scientific name plus where listed to account for both listed subspecies, distinct population segments, and evolutionarily significant units) was considered for inclusion for a refuge unit if documents indicated it was:

  • known or believed to occur on the unit based on data or expert opinion; or
  • dependent on the refuge unit, such as the refuge protecting a water supply for a population off-unit.

Species found in the same county(ies) as the refuge unit but not listed in CCPs were given additional scrutiny, but not included unless we could find affirmative statements meeting the criteria above.

During the data collection process, we conducted multiple cross-checks of the data. This involved taking a random sample of refuge units and having a different team member than the primary data collector independently review the documents and data. We found occasional differences, typically attributable to differences of interpretation of prose, as well occasional administrative errors such as recording species next to the adjacent refuge unit in the spreadsheet. These errors were corrected and then the full dataset searched for additional examples where that may have occurred. While we have attempted to find all such errors, others may be discovered; please feel free to leave us a comment in this repository if you find a possible error.

This U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) feature layer depicts National Wildlife Refuges. The National Wildlife Refuge System administers a national network of lands and waters for the conservation, management and the restoration of the fish, wildlife, and plant resources and their habitats.


Blackwater National Wildlife Refuge

Data Currency: current Federal service (see ArcGIS REST Services Directory > National Wildlife Refuge System Boundaries)
Data Modifications: None
For more information: National Wildlife Refuge System
For feedback please contact: ArcGIScomNationalMaps@esri.com

Thumbnail image courtesy of: U.S. Department of Agriculture

A-16 Data Set

This data set is part of the Office of Management and Budget's Circular A-16 "Cadastre Theme".  OMB Circular A-16 is a federal government circular created to provide guidance for federal agencies that create, maintain or use spatial data directly or indirectly.

The Wetland Management Districts feature layer is one of three feature layers that supports the Cadastral Theme's "FWS Interest" data set. The three feature layers depict lands and waters administered by the FWS in North America, U.S. Trust Territories and Possessions. It may also include inholdings that are not administered by FWS. The other two layers are...
  • Wetland Management Districts
  • Waterfowl Production Areas

These are resource grade mapping representations of the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service boundaries. For legal descriptions of the land represented here, contact the USFWS Realty Office. This map layer was compiled by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service. Although these boundaries represent lands administered by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, not all areas are open to the public. Some fragile habitats need to be protected from human traffic and some management areas are closed. The public is urged to contact specific Refuges or other conservation areas before visiting.

properties.description: Outreach pop up events. Programs are held by Minnesota Valley National Wildlife Refuge's Community Outreach and Engagement Team and community/non-profit partners. All programs hosted by Minnesota Valley National Wildlife Refuge's Community Outreach and Engagement Team are completely free for all community members to enjoy. Programs can be advertised on our Facebook or official website. The Minnesota Valley National Wildlife Refuge's Community Outreach and Engagement Team may even do free programming as a pop-up event in a local park or lake! Not everyone may be able to come to the refuge, so this is one way the Minnesota Valley National Wildlife Refuge's Community Outreach and Engagement Team is able to reach into the community in their own neighborhood.

properties.description:
This layer was used in an educational StoryMap created by US Fish and Wildlife Service and Natural Resource Damage Assessment and Restoration (NRDAR)  Program in collaboration with students at William and Mary. Layer created by Mary Lawrence Young, William & Mary collaborator to USFWS. The layer shows the 34-acre restoration area within the Great Meadows Marsh Wildlife Refuge in Stratford, CT. 
This layer was manually traced in ArcGIS Pro from aerial imagery courtesy of the United States Fish and Wildlife Service. 

For more information contact Anne Condon, anne_condon@fws.gov
